tytul: Queso fresco and queso blanco from pasteurized milk (PNW and NMSU recipes)
wstep: This card gives two tested Extension recipes: queso fresco with buttermilk and rennet (PNW539, also in NMSU E-216), and no-rennet queso blanco curdled with vinegar (NMSU E-216).

ostrzezenia.tekst: Queso fresco-type cheeses can support the growth of Listeria.
FDA recommends that people vulnerable to listeriosis avoid all queso fresco-type cheeses, even those made from pasteurized milk.
In the USA the risk of listeriosis for pregnant women is about 10 times higher than for the general population.

akapity: Make these cheeses only from pasteurized milk; raw milk must be pasteurized before it is used for cheese.
To pasteurize raw milk for queso fresco, PNW539 (WSU Extension) heats it in an uncovered pan to 145 °F (63 °C) for 30 minutes and then cools it below 90 °F (32 °C).
Temperatures below 145 °F (63 °C) do not kill harmful bacteria in milk.
If the temperature drops below 145 °F (63 °C), heat the milk again and start the 30 minutes from the beginning.
The PNW539 recipe uses 1 rennet tablet dissolved in 1/2 cup of cold water, 1 quart of pasteurized cultured buttermilk and 2 quarts of pasteurized whole milk from a cow, goat or sheep.

It also uses 7 teaspoons (2 tablespoons + 1 teaspoon) of white vinegar, of 5% acidity in the NMSU version, and 3/4 teaspoon of salt (the salt amount is from PNW539; the NMSU version gives a different amount).
Use whole or 2% milk, nothing with less fat.
Mix the buttermilk with the milk, add the vinegar and mix well.
Heat the mixture to 90 °F (32.2 °C), stirring often, take it off the heat and do not overheat it.
Add the dissolved rennet and stir for about 2 minutes.
Let it stand for 30–40 minutes without stirring until the curd is firm.
Cut the curd into 1-inch (2.5 cm) cubes and let it stand for about 5 minutes.
Heat the curds and whey to 115 °F (46.1 °C) without stirring, take the pan off the heat and let it stand for 5 minutes.
Pour everything through cheesecloth and let the whey drain for 5 minutes.
Form the curd into a ball and gently twist the cloth to squeeze out the whey.
Break up the curd, mix in the salt, let it stand for 5 minutes and squeeze again.
Form the cheese and refrigerate it; NMSU leaves it in the mold in the refrigerator overnight and then packs it in an airtight container.
NMSU uses 1 gallon (3.76 l) of pasteurized milk, 4.6 fl oz (137 ml) of vinegar of 5% acidity, 9.2 fl oz (274 ml) of distilled water, 1 teaspoon (4.6 g) of salt and spices to taste.
Heat the milk to 176 °F (80 °C) for 20 minutes.
Mix the vinegar with the water and add it slowly to the hot milk until the whey is semi-clear and the curd particles start to stick together and become slightly stretchy.
A piece of curd should stretch about 1 cm (0.39 inch) before it breaks; you may not need all of the vinegar.
Drain the curd in a cloth bag, work in the salt and spices, and press it; high pressure is not needed.
Seal the cheese in boilable bags and put them in boiling water for 5 minutes.
Queso fresco from the PNW539 recipe keeps in the refrigerator at 40 °F (4.4 °C) or lower for up to a week, or in the freezer for up to a month.
NMSU says sealed and boiled queso blanco may keep for several weeks in the refrigerator, but should be eaten as fresh as possible.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): the source does not say how many weeks, so eat queso blanco within 5 days, the lower end of the 5–7 days NMSU gives for soft cheese.
Listeria can grow at low temperatures, including in the refrigerator.
FDA names queso fresco, queso blanco and requesón among the cheeses that people vulnerable to listeriosis should avoid, whether made from pasteurized or unpasteurized milk.
Where possible, cook queso fresco-type cheese in a dish to an internal temperature of at least 165 °F (74 °C).
